young.html: Immanuel Kant lived his whole life in one city, Königsberg, in Prussia. People said he walked at the same time every day so exactly that neighbors set their clocks by him. But in his head he made a huge journey.

Kant noticed something about how we know things. Imagine you always wore blue glasses that you could never take off. Everything you saw would look blue. You could be sure, before you looked, that the next thing you saw would look blue, because the blue comes from the glasses.

Kant said our minds work a bit like that. Everything we experience comes to us arranged in space and time, and connected by cause and effect. That's why we can be sure of some things before we look, like that 7 + 5 will always make 12, or that every event has a cause.

young.name: gb-kant-lenses
young.cap: Turn the mind's "lenses" on and off and see what experience would be like without them.

young.html: Colored glasses. Look through a piece of colored cellophane or a colored bottle. Before you look at the next thing, predict its color. How did you know? Then talk about it: Kant said space and time are like glasses we can never take off. Can you imagine something that is in no place and at no time?

full.html: Kant (1724–1804) taught at the university in Königsberg for decades. At 57 he published the Critique of Pure Reason (1781; much-revised second edition 1787). It is one of the hardest books on this ladder, and one of the most influential. Kant said reading Hume woke him from his "dogmatic slumber": if all knowledge came from experience, how could we know anything to be necessary and universal?

full.text:
That all our knowledge begins with experience there can be no doubt. …

But, though all our knowledge begins with experience, it by no means follows that all arises out of experience. For, on the contrary, it is quite possible that our empirical knowledge is a compound of that which we receive through impressions, and that which the faculty of cognition supplies from itself (sensuous impressions giving merely the occasion)…
full.author: Immanuel Kant
full.ed: Critique of Pure Reason, Bohn's Philosophical Library (Project Gutenberg text)

full.html: Kant sorts judgments two ways. A priori means known independently of experience; a posteriori, known from experience. Analytic means the predicate is already contained in the subject ("all bodies are extended"); synthetic means it adds something new ("all bodies are heavy"). The big question of the book is: how are synthetic a priori judgments possible? Kant thinks mathematics ("7 + 5 = 12", "a straight line is the shortest between two points") and the first principles of physics ("every event has a cause") are exactly such judgments.

full.text: It has hitherto been assumed that our cognition must conform to the objects… Let us then make the experiment whether we may not be more successful in metaphysics, if we assume that the objects must conform to our cognition.

full.html: Like Copernicus, who explained the heavens by moving the observer, Kant explains necessary knowledge by looking at the knower. Space and time are the mind's forms of intuition, the way anything must appear to us. The categories, such as unity, substance and cause, are the mind's concepts for joining appearances into one experience. Both are needed:

full.text: Without the sensuous faculty no object would be given to us, and without the understanding no object would be thought. Thoughts without content are void; intuitions without conceptions, blind.
full.work: Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Logic, Introduction

full.html: The price of this answer is a limit. We know things only as they appear to us, never as things in themselves. When reason tries to go beyond any possible experience, to prove that the soul is immortal, that the world had a beginning, or that God exists, it falls into illusions and contradictions, which Kant sets out as the antinomies: equally strong proofs on both sides, for instance that the world had a beginning in time and that it did not. In Meiklejohn's translation, Kant says he must "abolish knowledge, to make room for belief": these questions can't be settled by theoretical proof either way, and he took them up again in his moral philosophy.

Thinking Kant said the world is made up by each person's imagination. He held that the forms of space, time and the categories are the same for every human knower, which is why science is objective and shared.

deep.html: The Critique started a long debate. German idealists such as Fichte and Hegel (in the next era) dropped the thing in itself and built vast systems on the mind's activity. Others objected that Kant's list of twelve categories looks arbitrary. When mathematicians later developed non-Euclidean geometries and Einstein used one in physics, many concluded that Kant was wrong that Euclid's geometry is known a priori of space, while Kant's defenders reply that his deeper point about the mind's part in experience survives.
Kant's distinction between the questions science can answer and those it can't still shapes how many people think about science and religion.
